items.title: Ses kaydı ve hafıza
items.text: A growing number of people are recording conversations with elderly relatives, and the results are almost never what the recorder expected. The instinct is to ask about history: the war, the move, the hard years. Those answers tend to be the least useful, partly because they have been told so often that they have hardened into a fixed shape, and partly because the important detail has usually been polished away. The recordings that turn out to matter are the ones where nothing happens. A description of a kitchen. The names of four neighbors on a street that no longer exists. How much a bus cost and what the driver did when somebody could not pay. These are the things nobody thinks to preserve, because they seem too ordinary to lose, and they are exactly what disappears first. There is a practical difficulty. Most people begin recording after a diagnosis, which is the worst possible moment: the subject is tired, the family is frightened, and the recording carries a weight that makes ordinary talk impossible. The advice that archivists give is uncomfortable but consistent. Start ten years early, while it still feels unnecessary, and ask about a Tuesday rather than a decade.

questions.q: Why are the history answers least useful?
options: They have hardened into a fixed shape
questions.note: "They have been told so often that they have hardened into a fixed shape."

questions.q: Which recordings turn out to matter?
questions.note: "The recordings that turn out to matter are the ones where nothing happens."

questions.q: Why is the ordinary detail lost?
options: It seems too ordinary to lose
questions.note: "They seem too ordinary to lose, and they are exactly what disappears first."

questions.q: Why is starting after a diagnosis bad?
options: The recording carries a weight that stops ordinary talk
questions.note: "The recording carries a weight that makes ordinary talk impossible."

questions.q: What do archivists advise?
options: Start ten years early and ask about a Tuesday
questions.note: Son cümle.

items.title: Turizmin iki yüzü
items.text: A coastal town of nine thousand people receives about four hundred thousand visitors a year, and the arithmetic of that produces effects that neither side of the argument describes accurately. The complaint that tourism destroys a place is too simple. Without the visitors the town would have the economy of the villages inland, which are emptying at a rate nobody defends. The claim that tourism saves a place is equally careless. The money arrives, but it arrives in a shape that the town cannot easily use: concentrated in fourteen weeks, spent mostly with firms registered elsewhere, and paid to staff who are themselves seasonal and leave in October. What the town is left with for the other thirty-eight weeks is a high street where two thirds of the units are shut and a housing market priced for people who are not there. The interventions that have worked in comparable places are unglamorous and local. A limit on how many properties in one street may be let to visitors. A requirement that a proportion of new building be sold only to residents. Neither policy attracts headlines, and both are considerably more effective than the debates that do.

questions.q: Why is the complaint too simple?
options: Without visitors the town would empty like the villages
questions.note: "Without the visitors the town would have the economy of the villages inland."

questions.q: What is wrong with the money that arrives?
options: It comes in a shape the town cannot use
There is too little of it
questions.note: "It arrives in a shape that the town cannot easily use."

questions.q: What is the town left with off-season?
options: Shut units and housing priced for absent people
questions.note: "Two thirds of the units are shut and a housing market priced for people who are not there."

questions.q: What kind of measures have worked?
questions.note: "The interventions that have worked... are unglamorous and local."

questions.q: What does the writer say about headlines?
options: The effective policies do not attract them
questions.note: Son cümle.

items.title: Sınav kaygısı
items.text: Exam nerves are usually treated as a problem to be removed, and a great deal of advice is built on that assumption. The assumption is only half right. A moderate rise in heart rate before a test improves performance measurably; the body is preparing to concentrate, and students who report feeling nothing at all tend to do worse than those who report feeling slightly sick. What harms performance is not the sensation but the interpretation. A student who reads a fast heartbeat as evidence that they are about to fail enters a loop in which the fear produces the symptom and the symptom confirms the fear. Studies that simply tell students the physical meaning of what they are feeling, without any relaxation technique at all, produce a small but reliable improvement in results. This is a cheap intervention and it is rarely attempted, partly because it sounds too easy to be serious. It also has an obvious limit. Reframing works on ordinary nerves and does nothing for a student whose anxiety is severe enough to stop them entering the room, and treating those two situations as the same problem is the mistake that the confident advice usually makes.

questions.q: What does a moderate rise in heart rate do?
questions.note: "A moderate rise in heart rate before a test improves performance measurably."

questions.q: What actually harms performance?
questions.note: "What harms performance is not the sensation but the interpretation."

questions.q: What do the studies do?
options: Tell students the physical meaning of the feeling
questions.note: "Studies that simply tell students the physical meaning of what they are feeling."

questions.q: Why is the intervention rarely attempted?
options: It sounds too easy to be serious
questions.note: "Partly because it sounds too easy to be serious."

questions.q: What is the limit of the method?
options: It does nothing for severe anxiety
It works only in one subject
questions.note: "Reframing... does nothing for a student whose anxiety is severe."

items.title: Tamir hakkı
items.titleEn: The Right to Open the Case
items.text: For about two decades it became steadily harder to repair the things people own. Cases were glued rather than screwed, parts were paired to a single device by software, and repair manuals were treated as commercial secrets. The manufacturers' argument was safety, and it was not entirely dishonest: a badly repaired battery is genuinely dangerous. The argument was also extremely convenient, since the same policies produced a replacement cycle that no marketing department could have achieved on its own. The change now under way came from an unusual direction. Rather than banning the practices, several governments required firms to publish a repairability score on the packaging, in the same place as the energy rating. Scores are crude and can be gamed, and within two years the average score rose sharply, which suggests that the gaming was less effective than the embarrassment. The remaining obstacle is not law but skill. A generation has grown up without ever opening anything, and a repairable device is worth little to somebody who has never held a screwdriver. The countries making the most progress are the ones that funded repair workshops at the same time as the labels.

questions.q: What made repair harder?
options: Glued cases, paired parts and secret manuals
questions.note: "Cases were glued rather than screwed, parts were paired... manuals were treated as commercial secrets."

questions.q: What does the writer say about the safety argument?
options: Not entirely dishonest but very convenient
questions.note: "It was not entirely dishonest... The argument was also extremely convenient."

questions.q: What did several governments require?
options: A repairability score on the packaging
questions.note: "Required firms to publish a repairability score on the packaging."

questions.q: What does the rise in scores suggest?
questions.note: "The gaming was less effective than the embarrassment."

questions.q: What is the remaining obstacle?
questions.note: "The remaining obstacle is not law but skill."

items.title: Yeni bir şehirde arkadaşlık
items.text: People who move cities in their thirties are routinely surprised by how hard it is to make friends, having found it effortless at twenty. The explanation is not that adults are colder. Friendship reliably requires three conditions: repeated unplanned contact, a shared activity, and enough time in one another's company for the conversation to move past the subject that brought people together. School and university supply all three without anybody arranging anything. Adult life supplies the first only at work, where the relationship is complicated by the fact that both parties are being paid to be there and one of them may one day be reviewing the other. The practical conclusion is unromantic and it is the only one that reliably works. Friendship in adulthood has to be scheduled, which feels wrong to people who remember it happening by itself. The activity matters less than its regularity: a class that meets weekly for eight weeks will produce more genuine connection than eight separate interesting evenings with different people. Those who understand this tend to describe the first year in a new city as a project rather than a disappointment, and they are the ones who are still there in year three.

questions.q: What are the three conditions for friendship?
options: Unplanned contact, a shared activity, and time
questions.note: "Repeated unplanned contact, a shared activity, and enough time."

questions.q: Why is work an incomplete substitute?
options: Both are paid to be there and one may review the other
questions.note: "Both parties are being paid to be there and one of them may one day be reviewing the other."

questions.q: What is the practical conclusion?
options: Adult friendship has to be scheduled
questions.note: "Friendship in adulthood has to be scheduled."

questions.q: What matters more than the activity?
questions.note: "The activity matters less than its regularity."

questions.q: How do successful people describe the first year?
options: As a project rather than a disappointment
questions.note: Son cümle.
